analysis.one_liner: Exempts livestock farms from Clean Air Act permits for animal-related emissions like methane.
analysis.headline: The bill drew three cosponsors — two Democrats and one Republican — and one committee hearing in September 2022, but never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend the Clean Air Act to bar the EPA from ever issuing permits for emissions that come from livestock's biological processes — carbon dioxide, nitrogen oxides, water vapor, and methane. In practice it would write a permanent exemption for livestock operations, including the largest ones, into federal law. It was introduced in April 2021 and sent to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which held a hearing in September 2022 but never voted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Livestock producers — above all large concentrated operations — would be spared Clean Air Act Title V permitting for the carbon dioxide, nitrogen oxides, water vapor, and methane that come from animals' biological processes, along with the permit costs, monitoring, and operating conditions that can come with a permit.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would amend the Clean Air Act so that no permit may be issued under a Title V permit program for any carbon dioxide, nitrogen oxide, water vapor, or methane emissions resulting from biological processes associated with livestock production.

It would relieve livestock producers of the costs and obligations that come with federal air permits — application fees, emission monitoring and reporting, and any conditions a permit would place on how a facility operates.

It would settle permanently, in the industry's favor, the question of whether biological emissions from livestock ever need a federal air permit, rather than leaving that decision to EPA case by case.

analysis.who_pays: People living near large livestock operations and the public generally, who would bear unmonitored air emissions — methane, nitrogen oxides — from livestock facilities with no federal permit process to track or limit them.
analysis.who_pays_short: Neighbors of large livestock farms, and the public

drawbacks.text: The exemption is not limited to small family farms: it bars a permit for any emissions from biological processes associated with livestock production, including the largest concentrated feeding operations.

It would remove a federal Clean Air Act check on methane — a potent greenhouse gas — and on nitrogen oxides that contribute to smog, leaving people who live near large livestock facilities without the permitting process that is the main federal mechanism for tracking and limiting those emissions.

Because the prohibition would be written into the Clean Air Act itself, it would tie the hands of regulators permanently rather than letting EPA weigh farm size, technology, or local air impacts case by case.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For livestock producers the benefit is concrete and one-sided: no federal air permits, no monitoring, no emission conditions for their animals' biological emissions, locked into law. The cost falls on people living near large operations and on the public, who would lose the federal permitting tool for methane and smog-forming emissions from a major source. An honest supporter might argue that subjecting diffuse farm emissions to industrial-style permitting is impractical and could burden family farms; the counter is that the bill draws no size line and writes a blanket, permanent exemption rather than a tailored one. As introduced, the bill never got far enough for this trade-off to be tested in a hearing-driven rewrite or a vote.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee; the committee held one hearing but never voted on it, and the two-year Congress ended without Senate action.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 29, 2021, read twice, and referred to the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works the same day.
The committee held hearings on the bill on September 7, 2022, printed as S.Hrg. 117-571, but never voted to send it to the Senate floor.
No further action was taken before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, so the bill never received a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained anything concrete. EPA was not requiring permits for livestock biological emissions, so livestock producers avoided nothing they currently face — while the public keeps the Clean Air Act's existing authority over those emissions, unused but intact.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nobody concretely; the public keeps existing Clean Air Act authority

for.name: Sen. John Thune
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and spoke on introduction; the Senate read it twice and sent it to committee the same day.

for.name: Sen. Kyrsten Sinema
for.what_they_did: Original cosponsor; the bill was introduced 'for himself and Ms. Sinema.'

against.name: Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works
against.what_they_did: Held one hearing on the bill in September 2022 but never voted to report it to the full Senate.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship — a Republican lead author with a Democratic original cosponsor and three cosponsors in all — but no vote was ever held, so no party split shows up in the record.

industries.industry: Livestock producers (cattle, hog, and poultry operations, including large concentrated feeding operations)
industries.note: The bill would exempt their biological emissions — methane, carbon dioxide, nitrogen oxides, water vapor — from any Clean Air Act Title V permit, sparing them permit costs, monitoring, and emission conditions. That gain comes at the expense of neighbors of large operations, who would lose a federal check on air pollution from facilities they live near.
